246.title: Al-Fattah, the Opener
246.hook: the Opener, of doors, of hearts, of ways out
246.howItsDone: Many Muslims say Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik, O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy, when entering a mosque, and call on al-Fattah when a matter is stuck, asking for an opening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Razzaq: the birds out hungry and back full, and the camel tied. Your line was provided for.

Remember Hudaybiyyah, eleven days ago, where the name ar-Rahman was struck from the treaty's first line? The rest of it felt worse. The Muslims had come to visit the Ka'ba and were sent home without reaching it. Some of the terms looked one-sided. Many companions were deeply upset; Umar, Bukhari records, went to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asking why they should accept such terms. They rode back toward Medina with their heads down. On the way, a surah came down, and its first line called that treaty a clear victory. The Arabic word for victory there is the same word as opening.
screen: `SENT HOME FROM MECCA.` → `A TREATY THAT FELT LIKE A LOSS.` → `CALLED A CLEAR VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Inna fatahna laka fathan mubina. The first line of Surah al-Fath: We have opened for you a clear opening, a clear victory. The root is f-t-h, to open. It gives miftah, a key. It gives fath, an opening, and a victory, because a victory is a way through. And it gives the name of the first surah you learned: al-Fatiha, the opening. The treaty that looked like a door slamming turned out to be a door opening: two years of peace, in which, historians say, more people entered Islam than in all the years before. Al-Fattah is the one who opens. In Surah Saba' the name has a second shade: our Lord will bring us together, then He will open between us with truth, and He is al-Fattah, al-'Alim, the Opener, the All-Knowing. Here opening means judging: laying a dispute open so the truth is seen. In Surah Fatir, whatever mercy Allah opens for people, no one can hold back; whatever He holds back, no one can release. In al-An'am: with Him are the keys of the unseen. So the name covers every kind of stuck: a locked door, a locked-up heart, a dispute no one can settle, a way out you can't see. Entering a mosque, many Muslims say words the Prophet taught, recorded by Muslim: O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy. The one entering asks; the opening is left to al-Fattah.
screen: `FATH — AN OPENING, A VICTORY.` · `MIFTAH, FATH, AL-FATIHA.` · `OPENING THE TRUTH BETWEEN PEOPLE.` · `THE KEYS OF THE UNSEEN.` · then, large: `THE OPENER.`

segments.voice: Name one thing in your life that feels stuck, a conversation going nowhere, a job search, a friendship gone cold, something in you that won't budge, and picture it as a closed door. Don't push on it; stand in front of it, breathe, and let not holding the key be a relief instead of a fear. If you pray, you can ask Allah, al-Fattah, to open it, or to open another way you haven't seen.
Al-Fattah. The Opener, of doors, hearts and ways out, and the one who opens the truth between people. Today's word.
Your line: the opener. A treaty that felt like a loss was called a clear opening. Day two hundred forty-six is yours.

the one who closes every door for good
the one who begins every new thing

247.title: Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing
247.hook: the All-Knowing, who knows what the heart hides
247.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a, personal prayer, in any language and at any time, often quietly, following the example of prophets like Zakariyya; some save the night, or the prostration of the prayer, for what they have told no one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Fattah: the treaty that felt like a loss and was called a clear opening. Your line was the opener.

Some things people carry and never say out loud. A fear. A hope that feels too big or too silly. Something they did. Something done to them. It sits in a back room of the heart, and it's easy to get very good at walking past the door. Surah Maryam begins with an old man going through that door. Zakariyya, a prophet, his bones weak, his hair gone white, his wife unable to have children. He calls on his Lord, the surah says, with a cry in secret, a hidden call. Today: Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing.
screen: `ONE THING NEVER SAID OUT LOUD.` → `AN OLD MAN, GRAY AND WEAK.` → `A HIDDEN CALL.`

segments.voice: What Zakariyya says is simple and raw: my bones have grown weak, my head is shining with gray, and I have never been disappointed in calling on You. I want someone to carry on after me. Then he waits. First, the name. Al-'Alim comes from the root '-l-m, to know. It gives 'ilm, knowledge; 'ulama', scholars; mu'allim, a teacher. The name often closes a verse like a signature: and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing. What does He know? Everything, the Qur'an says, but it keeps pointing at the small and the hidden. In al-An'am, not a leaf falls but He knows it. In Ta Ha, if you speak aloud, He knows the secret and what is even more hidden. In al-Mulk: He knows what is in the breasts; should He not know, the one who created? And in Surah Qaf, in Pickthall's words: We verily created man and We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein. So why did Zakariyya say it at all, if Allah already knew? Muslim teachers often put it this way: du'a isn't news delivered to Allah. It's the servant turning toward the one who already knows, and being changed by the turning. Zakariyya's hidden call was answered with glad news: a son, Yahya, John, a name the surah says was given to no one before him. In the surah's telling, the secret call from the back room had a listener the whole time.
screen: `MY BONES HAVE GROWN WEAK.` · `'-L-M — TO KNOW.` · `NEARER THAN THE JUGULAR VEIN.` · `DU'A IS TURNING, NOT INFORMING.` · then, large: `HE ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Somewhere you won't be interrupted, let your breath slow and let the back-room thing come forward, the one you haven't said to anyone, without fixing or explaining it. If you pray, tell Allah silently, in plain words, the way Zakariyya did; if you don't, say it to yourself honestly in the quiet, and let it be known by you. Then rest in what it's like for the thing to be said and not hidden.
Al-'Alim. The All-Knowing, who knows the leaf that falls, the secret and what's more hidden still: what the heart hides. Today's word.
Your line: he already knows. No performance needed for the one who knows the back room. That's two hundred forty-seven days.

248.title: As-Sami' and al-Basir
248.hook: the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, who hears whispers and sees the ant
248.howItsDone: Muslims call on God as as-Sami' and al-Basir in private du'a, often quietly or silently, and many say after rising from bowing in prayer that God hears the one who praises him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-'Alim, the All-Knowing, who knows what the heart hides. Your line was he already knows.

A woman in Medina has a bad problem at home. Her husband has said an old Arabian oath that leaves her neither married nor free. She comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she argues. She pleads. She complains, out loud, to God. His wife Aisha is in the same room, and she said later that she could not even hear all of what the woman was saying. It was that quiet. Then verses came down that begin: God has heard the words of the woman who argued with you about her husband. The person in the room missed some of it. The one she was really talking to missed none of it.
screen: `A WOMAN ARGUES HER CASE.` → `AISHA CAN'T HEAR IT ALL.` → `GOD HAS HEARD.`

segments.voice: As-Sami': the All-Hearing, from sam', hearing. Al-Basir: the All-Seeing, from basar, sight. In the Qur'an they often come as a pair at the end of a verse, like two notes of one chord. One verse, in Pickthall's old translation: "Naught is as His likeness; and He is the Hearer, the Seer." First it says nothing is like him. Then it uses two words people use about themselves. Many Muslim scholars read it as a guard rail: God hears and sees, truly, but not with ears and eyes like ours. Human hearing gets tired; His doesn't. Human sight needs light; His doesn't. A saying often repeated in Muslim teaching has God seeing a black ant on a black stone on a moonless night. A picture, not a verse, but it makes the point: nothing is too small or too dark. And the pair isn't only about being watched. When Musa and Harun, Moses and Aaron, are sent to face Pharaoh, they're afraid, and God tells them not to fear: "Lo! I am with you twain, Hearing and Seeing." That's comfort, not surveillance. The woman in Medina had no lawyer, no power, no loud voice, and a complaint so quiet the person in the room missed some of it. The chapter she's remembered in is named for her: al-Mujadilah, the woman who argues. The Prophet taught that when people call on God, they're not calling someone deaf or far away. Heard. Seen. Even the whisper.
screen: `SAMI' — HEARING. BASIR — SEEING.` · `NOTHING IS LIKE HIM.` · `I AM WITH YOU, HEARING AND SEEING.` · `THE WOMAN WHO ARGUES.` · then, large: `HEARD. SEEN.`

segments.voice: Let the room go quiet and find the loudest sound, then a quieter one under it, then the quietest you can catch: a fridge, a breath, a bird far off. Open your eyes, find the smallest thing in view, a crumb, a thread, a speck of light, and hold the faintest sound and the smallest sight together. If you pray, you can call on God as as-Sami', al-Basir.
As-Sami', the All-Hearing: one of the two names, paired with al-Basir, the All-Seeing, that travel together through the Qur'an.
Your line: heard, seen. Even where no one seems to notice: a meeting, a group chat, a kitchen. Back tomorrow.

249.title: Al-Latif, the Subtle
249.hook: the Subtle, the Gentle, who works in ways too fine to see
249.howItsDone: Many Muslims call on God as ya Latif in times of worry, and some repeat the name as a dhikr, asking for gentleness in something hard.

segments.voice: Yesterday, As-Sami', the All-Hearing, paired with al-Basir, the All-Seeing. Your line was heard, seen.

Some turns in a life only make sense from far down the road. A job falls through. A move nobody wanted. A friend who leaves. Years later, some people trace good things back to exactly that wrong turn, though nobody announced it at the time. Not every turn, and not for everyone. The Qur'an tells of a man who lived this at the scale of a whole life: a well, a slave market, a prison. When he finally looks back on all of it, with his family in front of him, he reaches for one name.
screen: `THE WRONG TURN.` → `YEARS LATER, LOOKING BACK.` → `ONE NAME FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Al-Latif comes from a root, l-t-f, that holds two meanings at once. One is fine, delicate, subtle, too thin to see. The other is gentle, kind, tender. A latif breeze is soft; a latif touch is careful. Scholars say the two meanings are joined in the name: his kindness reaches you by paths so fine you don't notice them. One verse puts the name right next to sight. In Pickthall's translation: "Vision comprehendeth Him not, but He comprehendeth (all) vision. He is the Subtile, the Aware." Subtile is an old spelling of subtle. You can't see him; he sees all the way in. Now the man: Yusuf, Joseph. Thrown in a well by his brothers. Sold as a slave. Falsely accused. Years in prison. At the end of his surah, he's in charge of Egypt's storehouses, his parents and brothers are bowing before him, and his childhood dream has come true. He doesn't say, I earned this. He thanks his Lord for bringing him out of prison, blames the rift on Satan rather than his brothers, and never mentions the well they threw him into. In the Qur'an's words, his Lord is latif to whom he wills: gentle, working in fine ways toward what he intends. In Yusuf's own telling, gentleness was at work the whole time, too fine to see from the bottom of the well. Not that nothing hurts; Yusuf's story hurts for a long time. But in this story, a gentle hand is at work inside the part that hurts.
screen: `L-T-F — FINE, AND GENTLE.` · `VISION COMPREHENDETH HIM NOT.` · `THE WELL, THE PRISON, THE WAIT.` · `MY LORD IS LATIF.` · then, large: `GENTLE BEYOND SEEING.`

segments.voice: Go back over the last seven days slowly and look for something small that went better than it might have: a conversation that softened, a delay that turned out to help, someone who texted at the right moment. Not miracles, fine things you'd normally walk past; stay with the one you find. If you pray, you can call God by this name, ya Latif; if not, just let yourself be grateful for it.
Al-Latif. The Subtle and the Gentle at once: kindness that works in ways too fine to see. Today's word.
Your line: gentle beyond seeing. Something gone a little sideways may not be finished yet. Day two hundred forty-nine, done.

250.title: Al-Halim, the Forbearing
250.hook: the Forbearing, who doesn't rush to punish
250.howItsDone: Muslims name God as al-Halim, often alongside al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, and many take the Prophet's advice not to get angry as a daily discipline, pausing, sitting down or making wudu when anger rises.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Latif, the Subtle and the Gentle. Your line was gentle beyond seeing.

Somebody cuts you off in traffic, and your thumb is already on the horn. A message lands in the group chat that's clearly about you, and your reply is half typed before you've finished reading. Anger is fast. People often end up admiring the ones with a gap in them, a pause between the sting and the answer: you say something awful, and they wait, and they don't hand it back. Scholars of early Arabic poetry say old Arabia had a word for that pause, and prized it in its chiefs. The Qur'an takes that word and makes it a name of God. Today: Al-Halim.
screen: `THUMB ON THE HORN.` → `THE PAUSE BEFORE THE ANSWER.` → `A NAME FOR THE PAUSE.`

segments.voice: Al-Halim comes from hilm. In old Arabia, hilm was the great virtue of a leader: calm, self-control, the power to hold back when you could strike. Its opposite was jahl. Jahl is usually translated as ignorance, but in the old poems it often means hot-headedness, the man who flies off the handle and starts a feud over an insult. So al-Halim is the One who sees every wrong, has all the power to answer it at once, and doesn't rush. The Qur'an says it plainly: if God took people to task right away for everything they earned, he wouldn't leave a single creature walking on the earth. Instead, he gives time: time to notice, time to turn around. Muslims hear forbearance in that delay, not indifference: al-Halim sees, and waits, because the waiting leaves the door open. The name often sits beside forgiving: first he holds back, then he forgives. And hilm is a name a person can grow into. The Qur'an calls Abraham halim. When a chief named al-Ashajj came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with his people, the Prophet told him, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, that he had two qualities God loves: hilm, forbearance, and anah, taking your time. Another man asked the Prophet for advice and was told, don't get angry; when he asked again, the same answer, again. Not that anger never comes. It just doesn't get to drive.
screen: `HILM — THE CHIEF'S CALM.` · `JAHL — THE HOT HEAD.` · `HE SEES, AND GIVES TIME.` · `TWO QUALITIES GOD LOVES.` · then, large: `SLOW TO ANGER.`

segments.voice: Bring back a moment from this week when something stung, and feel how fast the answer wanted to come. Now put a gap there, one slow breath in and one slow breath out, and only then picture what you'd say, noticing whether it's different; run it once more with another moment. If you pray, you can ask God, al-Halim, for a little of his hilm.
Al-Halim. The Forbearing: the One who sees every wrong, holds all the power, and doesn't rush to punish. Today's word.
Your line: slow to anger. One breath between the sting and the answer. Two hundred fifty days now.

251.title: Al-Wadud, the Loving
251.hook: the Loving, whose love is steady and shown
251.howItsDone: Muslims call on God as al-Wadud in du'a, and many understand love for others as something shown in deeds: gifts, visits, help, and a hadith that says to give gifts to one another so love grows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Halim, the Forbearing, who doesn't rush to punish. Your line was slow to anger.

Some people never say I love you. A father who gets up at five to scrape the ice off your windshield before you're awake. A grandmother who remembers you hate onions and quietly picks them out of your plate for thirty years. A friend who shows up to help you move and never mentions it again. You know the love because it keeps showing up, in the same shape, over and over. Arabic has more than one word for love, and one of them is exactly this: love you can see in what it does. The Qur'an uses it as a name of God. Today: Al-Wadud.
screen: `ICE SCRAPED OFF THE WINDSHIELD.` → `NO ONIONS, FOR THIRTY YEARS.` → `LOVE THAT SHOWS.`

segments.voice: You first met this name at Al-Buruj, on day two hundred five, sitting right after the Forgiving. Today, follow where that love goes. Arabic's everyday word for love is hubb. Wudd is different. Scholars of the language describe it as love that comes out: affection you can see, steady, like the ice scraper at five a.m. So al-Wadud is not only the One who loves, but the One whose love keeps showing. The Qur'an uses the same word between people, too. In Surah Maryam it says that for those who believe and do good, the Merciful will appoint wudd, love. Not a reward stored away for later. Love set down among them, here. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari shows how that love travels. When God loves a servant, He calls the angel Jibril: I love this person, so love them. Jibril loves them, and calls out to the people of heaven, and they love them. Then acceptance is set down for them on the earth. You've probably met someone like that: people trust them before they know why. So the name runs in two directions. Love comes down, steady and shown, and a person can pass it on by making love visible. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put it in the most ordinary terms, in a saying collected by al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad: give gifts to one another, and you will love one another. Not a speech. A deed.

segments.voice: Let a face come to mind, someone who'd never guess you're thinking of them, and choose one small deed you could do for them: make the tea, send the photo, fix the thing that's been broken. If you pray, you can call on God as al-Wadud, the Loving. Then just sit, and let yourself be loved for a minute.
Al-Wadud. The Loving: love that is steady, and shown, not only felt. Today's word.
Your line: loved. Love that is not only felt, but shown in what it does. See you tomorrow.

252.title: Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative
252.hook: the Appreciative, who rewards the smallest good
252.howItsDone: Many Muslims take the hadith of the thorny branch literally and clear obstacles from paths and roads, and the Prophet counted removing harm from the road as a branch of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Wadud, the Loving, whose love is shown. Your line was loved.

You held a door. You wiped the counter someone else left sticky. You moved the scooter off the sidewalk so the next person with a stroller wouldn't have to. Nobody saw. Nobody said thanks. Easy to file under: didn't count. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told of a man walking down a road who found a thorny branch lying across it. He moved it out of the way, so it wouldn't hurt anyone. That's the whole deed. And the hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, says God thanked him for it, and forgave him. God thanked him. For a branch. Today: Ash-Shakur.
screen: `NOBODY SAW.` → `A THORNY BRANCH ON THE ROAD.` → `GOD THANKED HIM.`

segments.voice: Ash-Shakur comes from shukr, the word for thanks from the very start of the path. A person with shukr is grateful. But God doesn't need anything from us, so what does it mean for him to be shakur? Scholars explain it as appreciation: he notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. A branch moved, a whole life forgiven. That's the scale. The Qur'an puts it in two short lines near its end. In Pickthall's translation: "And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then." In the Arabic it's a dharrah, a speck, some say the tiniest ant. Nothing is too small to be seen, and answered. And the Prophet backed it up in a hadith in Sahih Muslim: don't look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. A smile is on the list. Now look back at this week, because every name has pointed here. Al-Fattah opened. Al-'Alim knew what the heart hides. As-Sami' heard the woman in Medina. Al-Latif worked too finely to see. Al-Halim held back. Al-Wadud loved, and showed it. And Ash-Shakur notices the smallest thing you did, and doesn't let it disappear. Seven days, eight names, one picture running through them: in the Qur'an's telling, nothing a person does is too small, too quiet, or too hidden to count.
screen: `SHUKR — THANKS, FROM GOD.` · `AN ATOM'S WEIGHT OF GOOD.` · `EVEN A CHEERFUL FACE.` · `EIGHT NAMES THIS WEEK.` · then, large: `NOTHING SMALL IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Go back over today and find the smallest kind thing anyone did for you: the barista who remembered your name, the coworker who refilled the printer, the kid who put their plate in the sink without being asked. Choose one, and picture thanking them, naming the small thing so they know it was seen. If you pray, you can thank God for it too.
Ash-Shakur. The Appreciative: the One who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size. Today's word.
Your line: nothing small is lost. Not even a branch moved off a road. Day two hundred fifty-two, and a week of names, done.

options: step over it. not your branch.

tell someone else to move it.
fork.reveal: the man in the hadith moved it, and God thanked him and forgave him. the smallest deed, answered at full size.

original.note: Arabic: the Appreciative. from shukr, thanks: here, the One who rewards small good richly.

trapdoor: what you thought: we're supposed to thank God.
what it means: God is the Appreciative one, who notices the smallest good and rewards it far beyond its size.
what a scholar hears: the hadith uses the verb shakara of God: he thanked the man. scholars read God's shukr as reward, never as need.
